text: For the same diameter and thickness its developed area is the smallest of the dish end types: the crown is 0.785 ID², against about 1.084 ID² for a 2:1 semi-ellipsoidal head and 1.571 ID² for a hemispherical head. It carries less pressure for the same thickness, so it usually needs stiffening or a heavier plate.

The head is a flat circular crown with a straight cylindrical flange. The developed area is π × R² for the crown plus 2π × R × SF for the flange, where R is the inside radius, ID ÷ 2. Weight is that area × plate thickness × density: ID 1000 mm with SF 40 mm and T 6 mm in carbon steel gives 42.91 kg.

A flanged flat head is a flat crown bent down into a straight flange through a corner radius R. The crown stays at the level of the top of that bend, so its height above the tangent line where the knuckle turns vertical equals the knuckle radius. The flat crown diameter is then ID − 2R.

The crown is spherical with radius C.R and the knuckle is a torus of radius K.R. Where the two meet, the height above the tangent line is H = C.R − √((C.R − K.R)² − (R − K.R)²) with R = ID ÷ 2. The height is therefore calculated from the diameter and the two radii, not entered.

Each station is reported at its azimuth. Blank X and Y give the point on the blank circumference at that azimuth, so the rim can be divided into the same angles; the meridian length in the table is then stepped out along that radial line from the centre to place the station.

The dish is half an ellipsoid of revolution with semi-axes a = ID ÷ 2 and b = H. With e = √(1 − b² ÷ a²) the area is πa² + (πb² ÷ 2e) × ln((1 + e) ÷ (1 − e)); when the head is taller than it is wide (b > a) the same integral is evaluated with the inverse-sine form.

C.R = ID is the standard 100% crown proportion for torispherical heads, normally used with a knuckle of about 6% to 10% of the diameter. Fixing the crown radius leaves the diameter, the knuckle radius, the straight flange and the thickness as the only inputs.

No. The calculator develops the flat crown (πR²) and the cylindrical flange (2πR · SF); the small fillet surface of the knuckle is not added, which keeps the estimate marginally conservative. The knuckle still sets the drawing and the crown diameter.

Use the corner radius of your former or design drawing, typically a few per cent of the inside diameter. It must be smaller than the inside radius (ID ÷ 2) so that the flat crown ID − 2R stays positive; the field is validated on that rule.

They divide the circumference into 12 to 96 equal angular steps and control the station table and the radial lines drawn on the section and the blank. More divisions give a finer template; the area, blank diameter and weight do not change.

A double-curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching. The circle is the area-equivalent blank, 2 × √(A ÷ π): a flat plate of that diameter has the same surface area as the head, so it is the minimum plate size before allowances.

The height is the vertical semi-axis of the ellipsoid. A flatter dish (smaller H) has less surface for the same diameter, so the area, blank diameter and weight all fall; as H approaches ID ÷ 2 the area approaches the hemispherical 2πR².

The knuckle is a torus swept about the head axis: A = 2π × K.R × [(R − K.R) × θk + K.R × sin θk], where θk is the knuckle arc angle in radians. The arc runs from the tangent point to the start of the vertical flange.

The crown and the knuckle together have more surface than a flat disc of the same diameter, so the area-equivalent blank 2 × √(A ÷ π) is larger than ID. A production blank also needs a forming and trim allowance on top of that.

The calculator works on the inside surface, matching the inside diameter you enter. Using outside dimensions would raise the area by roughly 2T/R, which is small beside forming and mill tolerances for normal plate thicknesses.

Standard flanged and dished heads use about 6% of the inside diameter, and some specifications use 10%; for ID 1000 mm that is 60 mm to 100 mm. The value must stay below ID ÷ 2 and it is the radius labelled R on the drawing.

Yes, for the same diameter: H = 0.25 ID for a 2:1 ellipsoidal head, against about 0.19 ID for a torispherical head with C.R = ID and a 10% knuckle. The taller dish develops more area, so it weighs more at the same thickness.

The crown is the spherical zone of radius C.R above the tangent point: A = 2π × C.R × (H − K.R × sin θk). Only the part of the sphere above the knuckle is counted, so the crown area falls as the knuckle grows.

The dome is half a sphere with area 2πR², and the straight flange adds 2π × R × SF. Multiplying the total area by the plate thickness and the density gives the weight; at ID 1000 mm the dome alone is 1.571 m².

A half sphere is fully defined by its diameter: the crown height is the inside radius, H = R = ID ÷ 2. The calculator shows R as a calculated field beside the diameter, so the two can never disagree.
Its dome area is 1.571 ID², against about 1.084 ID² for a 2:1 semi-ellipsoidal head, so for the same thickness and material the dome is roughly 45% heavier before the straight flange is counted.
With no straight flange the dome area equals the area of a circle of diameter √2 × ID, so the blank is about 1.414 × ID: 1414 mm for ID 1000 mm. A straight flange increases the blank further.
A 2:1 head has D ÷ 2H = 2, so H = ID ÷ 4: 250 mm for ID 1000 mm. The results show the D ÷ 2H ratio of the values you entered, so you can confirm the profile before relying on the weight.

Yes. The straight flange is a cylinder of height SF below the tangent line with area 2π × R × SF, and it is added to the dish area before the blank and the weight are calculated.
No. The blank is the area-equivalent circle 2 × √(A ÷ π). Forming stretch, edge trim, weld prep and any thinning allowance are shop decisions and are added on top of it.
